title: Activated Sludge Troubleshooting and Solids Control
audience: Practising wastewater operators and supervisors seeking focused applied development.
prerequisites: Basic operator terminology, metric calculations and access to the source readings. Use a calculator; all supplied facility data are fictional.
introduction: Diagnose a fictional biological-treatment upset using consistent solids balances, settling tests, spatial oxygen observations and a monitored recovery plan. Practise distinguishing biomass loss from a change in process kinetics.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Solids inventory and retention boundaries
objectives: Calculate SRT with aeration and clarifier inventory.
Compare like-for-like solids bases and external losses.
modules.lesson:
### Why the boundary defines the number

Solids retention time is a mass balance statement, not a meter reading. You choose a control volume, you count the active solids mass held inside it, and you divide by the mass of solids leaving that volume every day by routes that actually remove solids from the system. Written plainly:

SRT (days) = solids mass inside the chosen boundary (kg) divided by solids mass leaving that boundary per day (kg/d)

Every argument about SRT on a plant floor is really an argument about the boundary. Two operators can measure the same tanks on the same day and report 15 days and 18 days, and both can be arithmetically correct, because one drew the boundary around the aeration basins only and the other included the clarifier sludge blanket. Neither number is wrong. What is wrong is comparing them to each other, or plotting them on the same trend line, as though the process changed.

The US EPA Process Control Manual for Aerobic Biological Wastewater Treatment Facilities, in its discussion of activated-sludge process observations, tests and interpretation, treats sludge age and retention time as interpretive tools that depend on consistent measurement practice. That is the core discipline here. A reproducible boundary that is slightly simplified beats a theoretically complete boundary that you compute differently every Tuesday.

The practical rule: write the boundary down, define it once in your standard operating procedure, and apply it every single calculation day. If you change it, mark the change date on the trend and keep both bases running in parallel for long enough to see the offset.

### What belongs inside the boundary and what does not

Inside the boundary, for a conventional activated sludge train, you normally have the aeration basin liquid volume, any anoxic or anaerobic selector zones that hold mixed liquor, and the secondary clarifier sludge blanket. Return activated sludge piping holds a small mass that most plants ignore, which is defensible if you ignore it consistently.

The returns are the part operators get wrong. Return activated sludge moves mass from the clarifier back to the aeration basin. It does not remove anything. A high return rate changes where the inventory sits, shifting mass out of the blanket and into the mixed liquor, which changes your measured MLSS without changing total inventory at all. That is exactly why an aeration-only boundary can make a return rate change look like a process change.

External losses are the routes that carry solids out of the secondary system for good:

- Waste activated sludge to digestion, thickening or haulage.
- Secondary effluent suspended solids over the clarifier weirs.
- Surface foam or scum wasted to a digester or to a solids handling process, if that route exists and is used.
- Clarifier washout during a hydraulic event, which is an unplanned loss and must be noted, not smoothed over.

Sidestreams returned to the headworks or to the plant influent are not losses from the plant, but they may be losses from the secondary boundary depending on where they re-enter. Trace the actual piping before you decide.

### The input register

Build the calculation from a fixed register so that a second operator can reproduce your number from the records alone. The table below is the working form. Values shown are placeholders for format only.

| Item | Source record | Units | Basis check | Common failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aeration liquid volume at operating level | As-built drawing or tank calibration record | m3 | Volume at actual weir or level, not tank top | Using full structural volume with a basin off line |
| MLSS concentration | Composite or grab, lab bench sheet | mg/L | Same basis as loss terms (TSS or VSS) | Averaging a settled sample |
| Clarifier surface area | As-built drawing | m2 | Number of clarifiers in service that day | Counting a unit that is drained |
| Blanket depth by layer | Sludge judge or blanket detector log | m | Depth measured at a defined location and time | One reading at the weir taken as plant-wide |
| Blanket concentration by layer | Core sample or RAS concentration proxy | mg/L | Stated as measured or as assumed | Assuming RAS concentration for the whole blanket |
| WAS volume | Meter totaliser, or pump run hours with drawdown-verified rate | m3/d | Matches the same 24 hour period as concentrations | Logbook estimate with no supporting record |
| WAS concentration | Sample taken at the actual waste withdrawal point | mg/L | Point matches the flow used | Using MLSS for a RAS-line waste |
| Effluent flow | Final effluent meter | m3/d | Same day, same period | Using influent flow when a bypass occurred |
| Effluent TSS | Lab bench sheet | mg/L | Compliance sample or process sample, stated | Substituting turbidity without a validated correlation |

Retain the bench sheets, the meter totaliser readings, the blanket log, and the calculation sheet itself. Under the Ontario Licensing guide for wastewater operators, in the material on operator-in-charge responsibilities and operating records, the operating record is the durable evidence of what was measured and what was decided. A process decision supported only by memory is not supported.

### Worked example 1: the same day, two boundaries

All values below are supplied case assumptions for this teaching example at a fictional plant. They are not authorized values and are not targets.

Given:
- Two aeration basins in service, each 1,800 m3 at operating level.
- MLSS = 3,200 mg/L.
- Two clarifiers in service, each 16.0 m diameter.
- Blanket layered: upper 0.50 m at 4,500 mg/L, lower 0.40 m at 7,000 mg/L.
- WAS from the RAS line: 95 m3/d at 7,000 mg/L.
- Final effluent: 7,400 m3/d at 12 mg/L TSS.
- All concentrations on a total suspended solids basis.

Step 1, aeration volume:
2 basins x 1,800 m3/basin = 3,600 m3

Step 2, aeration mass. Note that 1 mg/L = 1 g/m3:
3,600 m3 x 3,200 g/m3 = 11,520,000 g = 11,520 kg

Step 3, clarifier area:
Area per unit = 0.7854 x (16.0 m)^2 = 0.7854 x 256 m2 = 201.1 m2
2 units x 201.1 m2/unit = 402.2 m2

Step 4, upper blanket layer:
402.2 m2 x 0.50 m = 201.1 m3
201.1 m3 x 4,500 g/m3 = 904,950 g = 905 kg

Step 5, lower blanket layer:
402.2 m2 x 0.40 m = 160.9 m3
160.9 m3 x 7,000 g/m3 = 1,126,300 g = 1,126 kg

Step 6, total clarifier inventory:
905 kg + 1,126 kg = 2,031 kg

Step 7, total system inventory:
11,520 kg + 2,031 kg = 13,551 kg

Step 8, daily losses:
WAS: 95 m3/d x 7,000 g/m3 = 665,000 g/d = 665 kg/d
Effluent: 7,400 m3/d x 12 g/m3 = 88,800 g/d = 88.8 kg/d
Total = 665 kg/d + 88.8 kg/d = 753.8 kg/d

Step 9, SRT on each boundary:
Aeration only: 11,520 kg divided by 753.8 kg/d = 15.3 d
Aeration plus clarifier: 13,551 kg divided by 753.8 kg/d = 18.0 d

Answer: 15.3 days on an aeration-only basis and 18.0 days on a full secondary-system basis, from identical measurements. The gap is 2.7 days, about 18 percent.

Now look at a common shortcut. If you use aeration inventory only and count only WAS as the loss:
11,520 kg divided by 665 kg/d = 17.3 d

That is close to the full 18.0 day answer, but for the wrong reason. Two omissions, missing blanket mass and missing effluent solids, partly cancelled. On a day when the clarifier blanket climbs or effluent TSS deteriorates, the cancellation breaks and the shortcut drifts without warning.

### Worked example 2: mismatched bases

Same plant, same day, same inventory of 13,551 kg on a TSS basis. Supplied case assumptions again.

Error A, mixed liquor concentration applied to a waste sludge flow. WAS is drawn from the RAS line at 7,100 mg/L, volume 88 m3/d, but the operator multiplies the flow by MLSS:
Incorrect WAS mass = 88 m3/d x 3,200 g/m3 = 281,600 g/d = 281.6 kg/d
Incorrect total loss = 281.6 kg/d + 88.8 kg/d = 370.4 kg/d
Incorrect SRT = 13,551 kg divided by 370.4 kg/d = 36.6 d

Correct, using the concentration at the actual withdrawal point:
WAS mass = 88 m3/d x 7,100 g/m3 = 624,800 g/d = 624.8 kg/d
Total loss = 624.8 kg/d + 88.8 kg/d = 713.6 kg/d
SRT = 13,551 kg divided by 713.6 kg/d = 19.0 d

Answer: 19.0 days correct against 36.6 days from the mismatch. The error nearly doubles the reported SRT and would push an operator toward reducing wasting on a system that is already long.

Error B, volatile inventory against total losses. Suppose MLVSS divided by MLSS = 0.72 and the operator computes inventory on a VSS basis while leaving the loss terms on TSS:
VSS inventory = 13,551 kg x 0.72 = 9,757 kg
Mixed-basis SRT = 9,757 kg divided by 713.6 kg/d = 13.7 d

Answer: 13.7 days from mixed bases against 19.0 days like-for-like, an understatement of about 28 percent. A volatile basis is perfectly legitimate, and it is the more meaningful basis where inert solids loading is high or where nitrifier inventory matters, as discussed in the US EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual material on biological nutrient removal. It is legitimate only when both the numerator and the denominator are on that same basis.

### Reading the number and reading the change

| Observation | Likely explanation to test first | Evidence to pull | What not to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| SRT jumps up overnight with no wasting change | Boundary or basis changed, or blanket concentration assumption changed | Prior calculation sheet, blanket log, bench sheets | Do not increase wasting on one data point |
| SRT stable but MLSS falling | Inventory shifting into the blanket, or effluent solids loss rising | Blanket depth trend, effluent TSS trend | Do not chase MLSS with a return rate change alone |
| SRT drops sharply after a storm | Real washout loss over the weirs | Flow record, effluent TSS, clarifier observations | Do not treat the low value as the new steady state |
| SRT very long and nitrification fine, effluent solids poor | Possible dispersed growth or old sludge settling issues | Settleability test, microscopic observation | Do not assume long SRT is inherently safe |
| Calculated SRT disagrees with observed settleability and clarity | Suspect the inputs, especially WAS volume | Meter totaliser, pump run hours, drawdown check | Do not adjust the process to make the arithmetic agree |

What makes the number invalid: a WAS volume that is a guess; a clarifier mass built on a blanket concentration that was never measured and never labelled as assumed; concentrations and flows from different days; a unit counted as in service when it was drained; a mixed TSS and VSS calculation; and an effluent solids term omitted on a day when the clarifiers were struggling.

SRT is a trend instrument. One value tells you very little. Seven consecutive values on an unchanged boundary, read beside temperature, settleability and effluent quality, tell you a great deal.

### Common errors

1. Counting return activated sludge as a loss. RAS is internal recirculation. Including it in the denominator inflates the daily loss enormously and collapses the calculated SRT to a meaningless small number. The only solids leaving through the return line are the ones diverted to waste.
2. Multiplying a waste flow by the wrong concentration. Waste sludge drawn from a RAS line or a thickener underflow is far more concentrated than mixed liquor. Using MLSS with that flow understates the mass wasted and overstates SRT, as shown in Example 2. Sample at the actual withdrawal point, over the actual wasting period.
3. Turning a blanket depth into a mass without geometry or concentration. A depth reading alone is not inventory. You need surface area, the number of units in service, and a concentration for each layer. If a layer concentration is assumed rather than measured, write the word assumed on the calculation sheet so the next operator can weigh it.
4. Silently changing the boundary. Adding clarifier inventory partway through a month creates a step change in the trend that looks like process drift. Date the change and keep the old basis in parallel.
5. Treating a calculated SRT as a wasting setpoint. The calculation describes the system. Wasting decisions belong to your facility procedure, your approval conditions and your judgment about temperature, nitrification and clarifier capacity.

### What to verify before you act

Before you change wasting on the strength of an SRT calculation, consult the following. Do not substitute a general figure from any manual, including United States technical guidance, for the documents that actually govern your plant.

- The facility Environmental Compliance Approval for the sewage works, which sets the effluent requirements and operating conditions that apply to your site. Ontario effluent requirements are receiving-water based and can be more stringent than any general figure quoted in a textbook or a design manual.
- Your plant standard operating procedure for solids inventory and SRT, specifically the defined boundary, the sampling locations, the basis, TSS or VSS, and the calculation form.
- The tank calibration or as-built volume record, and the current unit status log confirming which basins and clarifiers were in service for the day in question.
- The WAS flow verification record. A meter with a current calibration record, or pump run hours combined with a documented drawdown test, is evidence. A logbook estimate is not.
- The sampling and analysis plan and the laboratory bench sheets, including any quality control flags on the MLSS, WAS and effluent TSS results.
- The operating record requirements described in the Ontario Licensing guide for wastewater operators under operator-in-charge responsibilities and operating records, so that your inputs, your calculation and your decision are all documented and attributable.

If any input fails verification, fix the input before you touch the process. Record what you rejected and why. An SRT you can defend from the records is worth more than a precise-looking number nobody can reproduce.

### Fictional worked scenario

All facility names, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are supplied for this teaching example only. None of the values are authorized limits, targets or setpoints.

**Setting.** Kettle Creek Water Pollution Control Plant, fictional, conventional activated sludge. The night operator, fictional, must report an SRT on the plant's defined boundary, which is aeration basins plus secondary clarifier blanket, total suspended solids basis.

**Supplied records for 14 March.**
- Aeration: two basins in service, 1,500 m3 each at operating level. MLSS 2,850 mg/L.
- Clarifiers: two in service, 14.0 m diameter each. Blanket 0.60 m at an average measured core concentration of 6,200 mg/L.
- WAS pump: rated 9.2 L/s, drawdown verified last month. Run time counter 2.6 h for the day. Sample at the WAS withdrawal point 6,400 mg/L.
- Day shift logbook entry: "WAS 120 m3/d, as usual." No meter totaliser reading, no run-hour support.
- Final effluent: 6,100 m3/d, TSS 9 mg/L.

**Record to reject.** The logbook entry of 120 m3/d is an unsupported estimate. The verified pump rate and run-hour counter give a defensible volume, so the logbook figure is rejected and the rejection is noted on the calculation sheet.

**Solution.**

Aeration mass:
2 x 1,500 m3 = 3,000 m3
3,000 m3 x 2,850 g/m3 = 8,550,000 g = 8,550 kg

Clarifier mass:
Area each = 0.7854 x (14.0 m)^2 = 153.9 m2; two units = 307.8 m2
307.8 m2 x 0.60 m = 184.7 m3
184.7 m3 x 6,200 g/m3 = 1,145,140 g = 1,145 kg

Inventory:
8,550 kg + 1,145 kg = 9,695 kg

WAS volume from verified data:
9.2 L/s x 3,600 s/h x 2.6 h = 86,112 L = 86.1 m3/d
WAS mass = 86.1 m3/d x 6,400 g/m3 = 551,040 g/d = 551 kg/d

Effluent mass:
6,100 m3/d x 9 g/m3 = 54,900 g/d = 54.9 kg/d

Total loss = 551 kg/d + 54.9 kg/d = 605.9 kg/d
SRT = 9,695 kg divided by 605.9 kg/d = 16.0 d

**Effect of the rejected record.** Using 120 m3/d: 120 m3/d x 6,400 g/m3 = 768 kg/d; total loss 822.9 kg/d; SRT = 9,695 divided by 822.9 = 11.8 d. The unsupported entry would have understated SRT by 4.2 days and could have prompted an unnecessary cut in wasting.

**Reported.** SRT 16.0 days on the defined boundary. Retain the bench sheets, run-hour reading, blanket log and the note rejecting the logbook estimate.

activities.instruction: Study the lesson and reproduce the worked example.
Read the source sections and note one application limit.
Work through the case evidence and prepare for the graded exercise.
Compare one decision with an alternative interpretation, then self-check it against the case evidence and exercise feedback. Optional notes can capture your reasoning; count only active work.
Complete the checks and review feedback.

checks.prompt: Two operators measure the same fictional activated sludge train on the same day and report SRT values of 15.3 d and 18.0 d. Both sets of arithmetic check out. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: One drew the control boundary around aeration only, the other included the clarifier blanket
One used the influent flow meter while the other used the final effluent flow meter reading
One sampled MLSS in the morning and the other sampled the same basin late in the afternoon
One reported sludge volume index while the other reported the food to microorganism ratio
checks.explanation: SRT is a mass balance over a chosen control volume, so including or excluding blanket mass shifts the answer without any process change. Sample timing can nudge MLSS slightly but would not usually create a gap of roughly 18 percent between two correct calculations.

checks.prompt: Return activated sludge carries solids from the secondary clarifier back to the head of the aeration basin. How should the RAS stream be treated when computing SRT for the secondary system?
choices: As a loss term, since solids physically leave the clarifier each day
Not as a loss, since it only moves inventory inside the boundary
As half a loss term, since roughly half the solids settle out again
As a loss only when the RAS rate exceeds the plant influent flow
checks.explanation: RAS redistributes mass between the blanket and the mixed liquor but removes nothing from the secondary system, so it never belongs in the denominator. Treating it as a loss would make a simple pumping change look like a large process change.

checks.prompt: Which of the following is an external loss of solids from the secondary treatment boundary?
choices: Mixed liquor recycled from the aerobic zone back to the anoxic zone
Return activated sludge pumped from the clarifier hopper to the basin
Waste activated sludge pumped from the RAS line to sludge thickening
Solids settling from the mixed liquor into the clarifier sludge blanket
checks.explanation: Wasting to thickening carries solids out of the secondary system for good, so it belongs in the daily loss term. Internal recycles and settling only move mass from one part of the boundary to another and must not be counted as losses.

checks.prompt: Supplied case assumption at a fictional plant: two aeration basins are in service, each holding 1,750 m3 at operating level, and MLSS is 2,600 mg/L. What is the aeration basin solids inventory?
choices: 91,000 kg of suspended solids
910 kg of suspended solids
4,550 kg of suspended solids
9,100 kg of suspended solids
checks.explanation: Total volume is 3,500 m3 and 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m3, so 3,500 x 2,600 = 9,100,000 g, which is 9,100 kg. The 4,550 kg answer comes from counting only one basin, and the other two answers are decimal slips in the gram to kilogram conversion.

checks.prompt: An operator calculates secondary inventory from MLVSS but leaves the waste sludge and effluent loss terms on a total suspended solids basis. What is the effect on the reported SRT?
choices: It is understated, because a volatile numerator is divided by total losses
It is overstated, because volatile solids are more active than inert solids
It is unaffected, because the volatile fraction cancels out of the ratio
It is unaffected, provided the volatile fraction stays above 70 percent
checks.explanation: The volatile numerator is smaller than the total solids numerator while the denominator is unchanged, so the quotient drops. A volatile basis is legitimate, but only when both the inventory and every loss term are expressed on that same basis.

checks.prompt: A plant wants any second operator to reproduce the daily SRT number from the operating records alone. Which practice most directly supports that goal?
choices: Average the aeration-only result and the full secondary result before logging
Define one boundary in the standard operating procedure and apply it daily
Log turbidity in place of effluent TSS to shorten the laboratory turnaround
Recalculate with the most theoretically complete boundary available each day
checks.explanation: A written, fixed boundary applied every calculation day makes the trend reproducible and comparable over time. Rebuilding the boundary daily or blending two bases produces a number that no one else can reconstruct from the records.

modules.title: Settling, solids loading and competing mechanisms
objectives: Calculate SVI and a stated clarifier solids-loading measure.
Differentiate poor settling from hydraulic and return-flow effects.
modules.lesson:
### The cylinder and the clarifier are two different experiments

A settleometer or graduated cylinder holds a fixed mass of mixed liquor in still water for a fixed time. Nothing enters, nothing leaves, and there is no upflow velocity, no inlet energy, no wind shear, no density current and no sludge withdrawal. A secondary clarifier is a continuously fed thickener and separator. Solids arrive with the mixed liquor, water leaves over the weirs, and solids leave through the return and waste lines. The clarifier fails when the rate of solids arriving exceeds the rate at which the sludge can settle and be removed, and that can happen with sludge that settles perfectly well in a cylinder.

This is why a single Sludge Volume Index value cannot diagnose a rising blanket. The US EPA Process Control Manual for Aerobic Biological Wastewater Treatment Facilities treats settling observations as one input among several, to be read together with microscopic examination, process loading, sludge age and clarifier performance. Use the same discipline. The cylinder tells you about the character of the sludge. The clarifier mass balance tells you whether the tank is being asked to do more than it can. Most contested troubleshooting calls come from mixing those two statements together.

A practical framing for your shift: settleability is a property of the biomass, solids loading is a property of the operation, and blanket depth is the outcome of both plus whatever the return sludge pumps actually delivered. Measure all three before you change anything.

### Calculating SVI so the number survives review

SVI is the volume in millilitres occupied by one gram of suspended solids after a stated settling period, normally 30 minutes, in a stated vessel. The formula requires consistent units:

SVI, mL/g = (settled sludge volume at 30 min, mL/L) ÷ (MLSS, g/L)

The two most common ways to produce a wrong SVI are leaving MLSS in mg/L and comparing a diluted result with an undiluted result. Both are shown below.

**Worked example 1 (supplied case assumptions, fictional plant data).**

Supplied values: settled sludge volume after 30 minutes in a 1 L graduated cylinder, SSV30 = 720 mL/L. MLSS from the same grab sample = 3,850 mg/L. A parallel test was run on a 1:1 dilution of the same mixed liquor with filtered final effluent, giving SSV30 = 310 mL/L on the diluted cylinder.

Step 1, convert MLSS to g/L:
3,850 mg/L ÷ 1,000 mg/g = 3.85 g/L

Step 2, undiluted SVI:
SVI = 720 mL/L ÷ 3.85 g/L
SVI = 187.0 mL/g

Step 3, the solids concentration in the diluted cylinder:
3.85 g/L × (1 part mixed liquor ÷ 2 parts total) = 1.925 g/L

Step 4, diluted SVI:
SVI(diluted) = 310 mL/L ÷ 1.925 g/L
SVI(diluted) = 161.0 mL/g

**Answer: undiluted SVI is 187 mL/g and the 1:1 diluted SVI is 161 mL/g on the same sludge, on the same day.**

The 26 mL/g gap is not an error. It is hindered settling and wall effect. When the settled volume at 30 minutes is a large fraction of the cylinder, the blanket compresses against itself and the cylinder wall, which inflates the undiluted index. That is exactly why a facility that trends undiluted SVI must keep trending undiluted SVI, with the same cylinder, the same mixing, the same settling time and the same temperature handling. Switching to a diluted method mid-trend creates a step change in the data that looks like a process improvement and is not.

Also record the sludge blanket interface behaviour, not only the final number. Note the time to first clear interface, whether the interface is sharp or diffuse, whether solids pin-floc off the top, and the clarity of the supernatant. A sludge at 187 mL/g with a sharp interface and clear supernatant is a different operating problem from 187 mL/g with a cloudy, straggler-laden supernatant.

### Solids loading on the clarifier

Solids loading rate, as used in this module, is the mass of suspended solids applied to the clarifier surface per unit time, based on the total feed to the tank, which is forward flow plus return activated sludge flow. State this convention in writing every time you report a value, because a forward-flow-only convention produces a smaller number for the same tank and the two are routinely confused in shift logs.

SLR, kg/(m²·d) = [(Q + Q_RAS), m³/d × MLSS, kg/m³] ÷ (clarifier surface area in service, m²)

Note that 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m³ equals 0.001 kg/m³, so MLSS of 3,850 mg/L is 3.85 kg/m³.

**Worked example 2 (supplied case assumptions, fictional plant data).**

Supplied values: average daily forward flow Q = 9,600 m³/d. RAS flow Q_RAS = 6,720 m³/d, taken from a magnetic flow meter calibrated within the facility programme. MLSS = 3,850 mg/L. Two circular secondary clarifiers, each 18.0 m diameter, both in service.

Step 1, surface area of one clarifier:
A = π ÷ 4 × (18.0 m)²
A = 0.7854 × 324.0 m²
A = 254.5 m²

Step 2, total area in service:
254.5 m² × 2 = 509.0 m²

Step 3, total feed flow:
9,600 m³/d + 6,720 m³/d = 16,320 m³/d

Step 4, solids mass applied per day:
16,320 m³/d × 3.85 kg/m³ = 62,832 kg/d

Step 5, solids loading rate:
SLR = 62,832 kg/d ÷ 509.0 m²
SLR = 123.4 kg/(m²·d)

Step 6, express per hour if your reference basis uses hours:
123.4 kg/(m²·d) ÷ 24 h/d = 5.14 kg/(m²·h)

Step 7, the separate hydraulic measure, surface overflow rate on forward flow only:
SOR = 9,600 m³/d ÷ 509.0 m²
SOR = 18.9 m³/(m²·d)

**Answer: 123.4 kg/(m²·d), or 5.14 kg/(m²·h), with a forward-flow surface overflow rate of 18.9 m³/(m²·d).**

Now change one condition. Take clarifier 2 out of service for weir repair and hold everything else constant:

SLR = 62,832 kg/d ÷ 254.5 m²
SLR = 246.9 kg/(m²·d)

The loading doubles instantly. The sludge did not change, the SVI did not change, and the microscopy would not change. If the blanket climbs that afternoon, settleability is not the cause. This is the single most useful judgment in the module: before you attribute a blanket to sludge quality, recompute the loading for the actual area, actual flow and actual RAS rate in service at the time.

### The return sludge mass balance as a lie detector

Under steady conditions, the solids entering the clarifier leave in the underflow, so the expected RAS concentration follows from a simple balance:

Expected RAS TSS, kg/m³ = MLSS, kg/m³ × [(Q + Q_RAS) ÷ Q_RAS]

Using the example 2 values:
Ratio = 16,320 m³/d ÷ 6,720 m³/d = 2.429
Expected RAS TSS = 3.85 kg/m³ × 2.429 = 9.35 kg/m³ = 9,350 mg/L

If the laboratory reports RAS TSS at 5,200 mg/L while the meter says 6,720 m³/d, the two records cannot both be right at steady state. Either the RAS flow is higher than logged, the sample was taken from a line that was not pumping, the blanket is inventorying solids rather than passing them through, or the meter is out of calibration. Rework the balance for the measured RAS TSS:

Implied Q_RAS = (Q × MLSS) ÷ (RAS TSS − MLSS)
Implied Q_RAS = (9,600 m³/d × 3.85 kg/m³) ÷ (5.20 kg/m³ − 3.85 kg/m³)
Implied Q_RAS = 36,960 kg/d ÷ 1.35 kg/m³
Implied Q_RAS = 27,378 m³/d

That implied return rate is far above the logged value, which tells you the recorded pair is inconsistent rather than telling you the true answer. Treat it as a data integrity finding and go verify the meter, the sample point and the pump status before you touch the process.

### Discriminating observations

| Observation pattern | Settleability driven | Hydraulic or loading driven | Return flow or equipment driven |
|---|---|---|---|
| SVI trend over 7 to 14 days | Rising steadily on consistent method | Flat | Flat |
| Blanket depth versus time of day | Elevated all day | Peaks with diurnal or wet weather peak, recovers overnight | Steps at pump start or stop |
| SLR recomputed for area actually in service | Within facility normal range | Elevated, often after a unit is removed from service | Normal |
| Measured RAS TSS versus mass balance expectation | Close agreement | Close agreement | Large unexplained gap |
| Effluent TSS character | Dispersed fines or filamentous carryover | Sheeting or washout at peak flow | Sudden carryover on one tank only |
| Supernatant in the cylinder | Cloudy or ashy | Clear | Clear |
| Response to a controlled RAS rate change | Little short term change | Little change | Blanket responds within hours |

Use the table as a sorting tool, not a verdict. A confirmed filament diagnosis requires qualified microscopic examination with documented method and observer, plus supporting process history such as sludge age, dissolved oxygen profile, septicity and nutrient conditions. A photograph and one SVI value are not a diagnosis. Chemical interventions of any kind, including selective oxidant addition to a return line, must be checked against the facility Environmental Compliance Approval and written operating procedures before they are even proposed.

### Input register for the settling and loading calculation

| Input | Units | Source of record | Validity check | Reject if |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SSV30 | mL/L | Settling test sheet | Same cylinder, same 30 min, dilution noted | Dilution not recorded |
| MLSS | mg/L | Laboratory bench sheet | Same grab, same time as settling test | Sample time differs by shift |
| Forward flow Q | m³/d | Plant flow record | Meter within calibration programme | Calibration overdue or meter flagged |
| RAS flow | m³/d | RAS meter or pump curve | Cross-check against mass balance | Balance gap unexplained |
| RAS TSS | mg/L | Laboratory bench sheet | Sampled while pump running | Line idle at sampling |
| Clarifier area in service | m² | Operating log plus maintenance record | Units confirmed in service that day | Log conflicts with work order |
| Blanket depth | m | Blanket finder or core | Same location and depth reference | Reference point changed |

### Common errors

**Dividing millilitres per litre by milligrams per litre.** Entering 720 mL/L ÷ 3,850 mg/L gives 0.187 and some operators then record 0.19 or, worse, move the decimal and record 19 mL/g. MLSS must be converted to grams per litre first. Any SVI below about 10 or above several hundred should trigger a unit check before it is trended.

**Using nameplate clarifier area when a tank is out of service.** The loading calculation in worked example 2 doubled from 123.4 to 246.9 kg/(m²·d) purely from area. Operators who pull the area from a design drawing rather than from the day's operating log will report a normal loading during an overload and will then go looking for a microbiological cause that does not exist.

**Comparing a diluted SVI to an undiluted historical baseline.** Worked example 1 gave 187 mL/g undiluted and 161 mL/g diluted on the same sludge. A methodology change reads as a 14 percent improvement. Document the method on every test sheet and note the change date prominently in the trend record.

**Sampling RAS from an idle line or a sample tap with settled solids in it.** The resulting concentration is meaningless, and it will corrupt the mass balance that you need to separate return flow problems from sludge quality problems.

**Acting on a single day's value.** Settling tests carry real variability from mixing, temperature and sample point. Two or three consistent days with the same method, read against loading and blanket data, support a decision. One reading supports another reading.

### What to verify before you act

Before changing RAS rate, wasting rate, clarifier units in service or any chemical addition, confirm the following records. First, the facility Environmental Compliance Approval and the operational plan or standard operating procedures, which define the units, flows, chemical additions and any performance conditions that apply to your works. Ontario sewage works operate to the specific terms of their own approval and the receiving water drives the effluent requirements, so no general figure from any manual overrides what your approval says. Second, the operating log and maintenance work orders for the day in question, to confirm which clarifiers, RAS pumps and meters were actually in service. Third, the calibration records for the flow meters used in the loading and mass balance calculations. Fourth, the laboratory bench sheets and chain of custody for MLSS and RAS TSS, including sample time and location. Fifth, the internal notification and authorisation pathway for any process change that touches an approval condition.

On record keeping and accountability, the Ontario licensing guide for wastewater operators sets out operator-in-charge responsibilities and operating record expectations. Your calculation is part of that record. Retain the raw inputs, the stated convention used for the loading measure, the dilution status of the settling test, the area in service, the arithmetic and the name of the person who performed it. For US technical framing, the US EPA Process Control Manual provides the interpretive background for settling observations, and the US EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual is useful for nutrient related process context, but both are United States technical guidance rather than Ontario requirements and neither sets your limits.

### Fictional worked scenario

**All facility names, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are supplied only as case assumptions for this teaching example. They are not authorized values for any real works.**

Maplecross Water Pollution Control Plant, conventional activated sludge, two circular secondary clarifiers each 20.0 m diameter. Night shift reports a rising blanket in clarifier 1 and high effluent turbidity.

Supplied records for 14 March:
- Forward flow, Q = 12,400 m³/d (meter calibrated 2 months prior)
- RAS flow logged = 9,300 m³/d
- MLSS = 2,900 mg/L
- SSV30, undiluted 1 L cylinder = 800 mL/L
- RAS TSS reported by lab = 3,100 mg/L
- Day shift log entry: "both clarifiers in service, SLR normal at 100 kg/(m²·d)"
- Maintenance work order 4471: clarifier 2 drained and isolated for weir repair, 12 to 16 March
- Day shift log entry: "filamentous bulking confirmed, recommend oxidant to RAS" with no microscopy sheet attached

**Records to reject.** The log claim that both clarifiers were in service conflicts with work order 4471. The maintenance record is the controlling evidence, so the SLR of 100 kg/(m²·d) is wrong. The "filamentous bulking confirmed" entry is unsupported: there is no microscopic examination sheet, observer or method, so it cannot be used, and no oxidant addition can be considered without checking the Environmental Compliance Approval and facility procedures.

**Worked solution.**

Area of one clarifier:
A = 0.7854 × (20.0 m)² = 314.2 m²

Total feed:
12,400 m³/d + 9,300 m³/d = 21,700 m³/d

MLSS in mass units:
2,900 mg/L = 2.90 kg/m³

Solids applied:
21,700 m³/d × 2.90 kg/m³ = 62,930 kg/d

SLR on the area actually in service:
62,930 kg/d ÷ 314.2 m² = 200.3 kg/(m²·d)

SVI:
800 mL/L ÷ 2.90 g/L = 275.9 mL/g

RAS mass balance check:
Expected RAS TSS = 2.90 kg/m³ × (21,700 ÷ 9,300) = 2.90 × 2.333 = 6.77 kg/m³ = 6,770 mg/L
Reported 3,100 mg/L does not reconcile, so the RAS flow record, sample point or pump status must be verified.

**Conclusion.** Loading is double what the log stated, driven by area out of service, and the return sludge record is internally inconsistent. The elevated SVI is real and worth trending on a consistent method, but the immediate defensible actions are to verify the RAS meter and sample point and to review the loading against the approval and procedures, not to dose a chemical on an unsupported diagnosis.

checks.prompt: Why can mixed liquor that settles well in a 1 L graduated cylinder still allow a rising blanket in a secondary clarifier?
choices: The clarifier is continuously fed and must settle and withdraw solids at the same time
The cylinder test always uses a warmer sample than the clarifier contents
Settled volume in a cylinder is measured in millilitres instead of litres
Clarifier weirs remove dissolved solids that the cylinder test cannot show
checks.explanation: The cylinder is a still batch test with no inflow, upflow or underflow withdrawal, while the clarifier fails when solids arrive faster than they can settle and be pumped out. Temperature can shift results slightly, but it is not the reason a good settling sludge can still overload a tank.

checks.prompt: An operator divides SSV30 of 640 mL/L by an MLSS value of 3,200 mg/L without converting units. What is wrong with the reported SVI?
choices: MLSS must be corrected to volatile solids before any SVI is calculated
MLSS must be expressed in grams per litre, so 3.2 g/L is the correct divisor
SSV30 must first be converted to litres per litre before the division
SVI requires a 60 minute settling period rather than a 30 minute period
checks.explanation: SVI is millilitres per gram, so MLSS in mg/L must be divided by 1,000 to give g/L, here 3.2 g/L for an SVI of 200 mL/g. Using volatile solids is a different index and is not part of the stated SVI convention.

checks.prompt: A facility that has trended undiluted SVI for two years switches to a 1:1 diluted settling method with no other change. What should the operator expect in the trend data?
choices: No change at all, since dilution cancels out in the SVI calculation
A gradual drift upward over several weeks as the biomass adapts
A step change to lower index values that does not represent a process improvement
A step change to higher index values caused by removal of wall effect
checks.explanation: Diluting relieves hindered settling and wall compression, so the diluted index reads lower on the same sludge, as in the worked example where 187 mL/g became 161 mL/g. Dilution does not cancel out, because both the settled volume and the solids concentration change but not in the same proportion.

checks.prompt: In this module, which flow basis is used when a clarifier solids loading rate is calculated and reported?

Return activated sludge flow only, since it carries the settled solids
Forward flow plus waste sludge flow measured at the wasting pump
Forward flow plus return activated sludge flow applied to the tank
checks.explanation: Solids loading here uses total feed, meaning forward flow plus RAS flow, and the convention must be stated in writing on every report. A forward-flow-only basis gives a smaller number for the same tank and is the most common source of confusion in shift logs.

checks.prompt: At a fictional plant the blanket climbs during the afternoon peak and recovers overnight, SVI has been flat for two weeks, and measured RAS TSS agrees with the mass balance. Which category does this pattern best fit?

Return flow driven behaviour caused by a failing RAS pump
Laboratory error in the daily mixed liquor solids result
checks.explanation: A blanket that peaks with flow and recovers overnight, with a flat SVI and an agreeing RAS balance, points to loading and hydraulics. A filament problem would show a rising SVI trend and an elevated blanket through the whole day, not overnight recovery.

checks.prompt: Supplied case assumption at a fictional plant: SSV30 is 260 mL/L and MLSS from the same grab sample is 2,600 mg/L. What is the SVI?

modules.lesson:
### What an ammonia result actually tells you

An effluent or final-cell ammonia number is a single point in space and time. It reports the residual left after whatever nitrifying population was present, at whatever temperature existed, with whatever oxygen and alkalinity were available, acting on whatever load arrived during the sampled period. It does not tell you which of those factors moved. Treat a rising ammonia result as a question, not a finding.

Start by separating the three things that can change an ammonia residual:

1. The nitrogen load arriving changed (mass, not just concentration).
2. The capacity of the biomass to oxidize that load changed (aerobic solids inventory, aerobic solids retention time, temperature, pH and alkalinity, dissolved oxygen availability, inhibition, or loss of biomass to the clarifier or to washout).
3. Nothing in the process changed and the number is wrong (sampling point, preservation, holding time, dilution, calibration, interference, or a composite that spans a period different from the one you are trying to explain).

The third category is not rare. US EPA's Process Control Manual for Aerobic Biological Wastewater Treatment Facilities, in its material on activated sludge observations, tests and interpretation, is blunt that interpretation depends on whether the test was representative. Before you change aeration, wasting or chemical addition, you should be able to say why you believe the number.

Spatial coverage matters as much as timing. A dissolved oxygen reading at the end of an aeration basin tells you about the end of the basin. In a plug-flow train the front third can be oxygen limited while the discharge end reads comfortably, because oxygen uptake is highest where load enters. If your only oxygen evidence is one probe at one location, you have not measured the oxygen profile and you cannot rank oxygen limitation against the other explanations.

### Keeping the basis consistent: as N, as CaCO3, as O2

Most nitrogen diagnosis errors are unit errors, not process errors. Three separate bases are in play in this module and they are not interchangeable.

- Nitrogen species are reported either as N or as the full chemical species. Ammonia reported as NH3 is roughly 1.22 times the same sample reported as NH3-N. Nitrate reported as NO3 is roughly 4.43 times the same sample reported as NO3-N. You cannot add or subtract species reported on different bases. In this module every ammonia and nitrate value is explicitly reported as N.
- Alkalinity is normally reported as mg/L as CaCO3. The nitrification stoichiometric factor used here is a supplied teaching factor of 7.14 mg alkalinity as CaCO3 consumed per mg of ammonia-N oxidized. The paired denitrification recovery factor used here is a supplied teaching factor of 3.57 mg alkalinity as CaCO3 returned per mg of nitrate-N reduced. These are theoretical screening factors for this example only. They are not site values and they are not dosing instructions.
- Oxygen demand for nitrification uses a supplied teaching factor of 4.57 mg O2 per mg of ammonia-N oxidized. Real oxygen requirement at your plant depends on synthesis yield, endogenous demand, carbonaceous load, alpha and beta factors, diffuser condition and basin geometry.

The stoichiometric result is a screening estimate of whether a mechanism is even plausible. It is not a prediction of final pH, and it is not a replacement for measured alkalinity and pH data.

### Worked example 1: theoretical alkalinity demand and residual screening

Supplied case assumptions for this teaching example only. Fictional plant, fictional readings.

- Plant flow: 6,800 m3/d
- Influent alkalinity: 220 mg/L as CaCO3
- Ammonia-N oxidized across the train: 22 mg/L as N
- Nitrate-N reduced in the anoxic zone: 8 mg/L as N
- Supplied nitrification factor: 7.14 mg CaCO3 per mg NH3-N oxidized
- Supplied denitrification recovery factor: 3.57 mg CaCO3 per mg NO3-N reduced

Step 1. Alkalinity consumed by nitrification, on a concentration basis.

22 mg NH3-N/L x 7.14 mg CaCO3 per mg NH3-N = 157.1 mg/L as CaCO3

Step 2. Alkalinity returned by denitrification, on a concentration basis.

8 mg NO3-N/L x 3.57 mg CaCO3 per mg NO3-N = 28.6 mg/L as CaCO3

Step 3. Net theoretical alkalinity change.

157.1 mg/L as CaCO3 consumed - 28.6 mg/L as CaCO3 returned = 128.5 mg/L as CaCO3 net consumption

Step 4. Theoretical residual alkalinity before other gains and losses.

220 mg/L as CaCO3 - 128.5 mg/L as CaCO3 = 91.5 mg/L as CaCO3

Step 5. Express the net demand as a daily mass, which is the form you need if chemical supplementation is ever evaluated under your approval.

128.5 g CaCO3/m3 x 6,800 m3/d = 873,800 g/d = 873.8 kg/d as CaCO3

Stated answer: the theoretical nitrification demand is 157.1 mg/L as CaCO3, net demand after the supplied denitrification credit is 128.5 mg/L as CaCO3, equal to 873.8 kg/d as CaCO3, leaving a theoretical residual of about 91.5 mg/L as CaCO3.

What the number means. A residual near 90 mg/L as CaCO3 in this example does not by itself indicate alkalinity limitation, so alkalinity would drop down the ranked list of explanations. What would move it back up the list is measured evidence: a measured mixed liquor alkalinity far below the calculated residual, or a measured pH depression in the aeration basin that tracks the ammonia increase. The US EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual, in its treatment of biological nutrient removal, discusses alkalinity and pH as design and operating considerations, but it is United States technical guidance and does not set Ontario requirements.

What makes this calculation invalid. If the ammonia-N oxidized figure was taken as the difference between an influent grab and an effluent composite, the 22 mg/L is not a real difference. If the anoxic zone nitrate reduction was assumed rather than measured, the 28.6 mg/L credit is fabricated and the net demand is understated. If influent alkalinity was reported as mg/L as HCO3 rather than as CaCO3, every line above is wrong by a factor of about 1.22.

### Worked example 2: aerobic solids retention time, oxygen demand and the load check

Supplied case assumptions for this teaching example only. Fictional plant, fictional readings.

- Two aeration cells, each 1,250 m3, total aerobic volume 2,500 m3
- Mixed liquor suspended solids in the aerobic cells this week: 2,900 mg/L
- Mixed liquor suspended solids two weeks ago: 3,600 mg/L
- Waste activated sludge: 95 m3/d at 7,200 mg/L
- Final effluent: 6,800 m3/d at 12 mg/L TSS
- Mixed liquor temperature fell from 18 degrees C to 12 degrees C over three weeks
- Influent ammonia-N: 28 mg/L as N at 6,800 m3/d

Step 1. Aerobic solids inventory this week.

2,500 m3 x 2,900 g/m3 = 7,250,000 g = 7,250 kg

Step 2. Solids leaving the system per day.

Waste: 95 m3/d x 7.2 kg/m3 = 684 kg/d
Effluent: 6,800 m3/d x 0.012 kg/m3 = 81.6 kg/d
Total: 684 kg/d + 81.6 kg/d = 765.6 kg/d

Step 3. Aerobic solids retention time this week.

7,250 kg / 765.6 kg/d = 9.47 d

Step 4. Aerobic solids retention time two weeks ago, same wasting.

2,500 m3 x 3,600 g/m3 = 9,000,000 g = 9,000 kg
9,000 kg / 765.6 kg/d = 11.76 d

Step 5. Change.

11.76 d - 9.47 d = 2.29 d lost, a reduction of about 19 percent

Step 6. Nitrogen mass load and theoretical nitrification oxygen demand.

28 g N/m3 x 6,800 m3/d = 190,400 g N/d = 190.4 kg N/d
190.4 kg N/d x 4.57 kg O2 per kg N = 870.1 kg O2/d for nitrification alone

Stated answer: aerobic solids retention time fell from 11.76 d to 9.47 d while mixed liquor temperature fell 6 degrees C, and nitrification alone accounts for about 870 kg O2/d at the stated load.

Judgment. Two conditions moved in the same unfavourable direction at once. Colder mixed liquor slows nitrifier growth rate, so the aerobic solids retention time needed to hold a nitrifying population rises exactly when your calculated value is falling. That combination is a far stronger explanation for rising ammonia than a single low dissolved oxygen reading. Note also that the 870 kg O2/d is nitrification only and sits on top of carbonaceous demand, so an aeration system that was adequate in summer may be at its limit in winter.

### Ranking competing explanations

Rank, do not declare. For each candidate explanation, write down the evidence that would confirm it and the evidence that would rule it out. Use this matrix as the working record.

| Candidate explanation | Supporting evidence to look for | Evidence that rules it out | Distinguishing test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Load increase | Influent ammonia-N mass up on a flow-weighted basis, hauled waste or industrial discharge received | Influent mass steady, flow steady | Recalculate kg N/d, not mg/L, over 7 to 10 days |
| Aerobic SRT loss | Falling MLSS, higher wasting, solids in effluent, clarifier upset | SRT stable within 10 percent | Aerobic solids inventory divided by total solids out |
| Temperature | Mixed liquor temperature falling, seasonal timing | Temperature flat | Plot ammonia against mixed liquor temperature |
| Oxygen limitation | Low DO at the inlet third, blower at maximum, fouled diffusers | DO profile adequate across full basin length | Multi-point DO profile at peak load, plus off-gas or blower amp trend |
| Alkalinity or pH limitation | Measured aeration basin alkalinity low, pH depressed and tracking ammonia | Residual alkalinity comfortable, pH stable | Measured alkalinity plus the Example 1 screening calculation |
| Inhibition or toxicity | Sudden onset, respiration rate drop, unusual upstream discharge | Gradual onset, normal respiration | Oxygen uptake rate comparison, upstream source check |
| Analytical or sampling error | Result inconsistent with nitrate and pH, no corroboration | Duplicate and second method agree | Resample, re-run, check calibration and holding time |

A useful ranking has one explanation clearly first, a second that is still live, and a named test that separates them. If three explanations are tied, you do not yet have enough evidence to act on anything other than the test.

### Common errors

1. Comparing concentrations instead of mass. Influent ammonia that rises from 24 mg/L to 28 mg/L during a dry spell with falling flow may be the same or less nitrogen load. Only kg N/d tells you whether load moved.
2. Taking the sludge age from the plant spreadsheet without checking what volume it uses. A total-system solids retention time that includes clarifier and digester inventory can be several days longer than the aerobic value that governs nitrification. Using the wrong one hides a washout.
3. Adding nitrogen values on different bases. Subtracting an effluent ammonia reported as N from an influent TKN reported as the full species, or comparing a nitrate reported as NO3 to one reported as NO3-N, produces differences that look like process failures.
4. Treating the 7.14 factor as a dosing instruction. It is a theoretical screening ratio. It ignores carbon dioxide stripping, sidestream returns, chemical addition upstream, and any alkalinity generated or consumed elsewhere in the works.
5. Using one end-of-basin DO reading to eliminate oxygen limitation, and doing it at 10:00 when the diurnal peak load arrives at 13:00.

### What to verify before you act

Verify the Environmental Compliance Approval for the sewage works and any operating manual or standard operating procedure written under it. Effluent requirements in Ontario are set in the approval for that specific works and are receiving-water based, so they can be more stringent than any general figure you read in a manual. Nothing in this module is a limit or a setpoint.

Before changing wasting, aeration or any chemical addition, confirm: the sampling plan and sample type for each value you are relying on, including location, composite period and preservation; the laboratory method and whether the result is reported as N or as the full species; the calibration and verification records for the dissolved oxygen and pH instruments used; whether any chemical addition is permitted by the approval and within the approved rate and point of addition; and the operating manual procedure for wasting rate changes. Where the Ontario licensing guide for wastewater operators addresses operator-in-charge responsibilities and operating records, the expectation is that the person making the adjustment is authorized to do so and that the record shows it.

### Records and evidence to retain

Retain the raw inputs, not only the conclusion. The defensible file for a nitrogen diagnosis contains: flow and ammonia-N results with sample type and time; the aerobic volume used and where that figure came from; MLSS and WAS concentrations with sample times; effluent TSS; mixed liquor temperature and pH; the dissolved oxygen profile with probe identification and calibration date; measured alkalinity; the arithmetic for each calculation with units shown; the ranking matrix with the rejected explanations and the reason each was rejected; and the operator-in-charge entry recording what was changed, when, by whom and under which procedure. A calculation without its inputs cannot be audited, and an adjustment without a recorded reason cannot be defended later.

### Fictional worked scenario

All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are used for training only. No value here is an authorized limit or setpoint.

The fictional Cedar Hollow Water Pollution Control Plant, a conventional activated sludge works, records rising final effluent ammonia over twelve days. Operator-in-charge B. Nantel assembles the file.

Supplied values:

- Average daily flow: 5,400 m3/d
- Influent ammonia-N: 26 mg/L as N (24 hour flow-weighted composite)
- Influent alkalinity: 190 mg/L as CaCO3
- Aerobic volume: 2,000 m3
- MLSS in aerobic cells: 2,150 mg/L
- WAS: 78 m3/d at 6,400 mg/L
- Effluent TSS: 15 mg/L
- Mixed liquor temperature: 11.5 degrees C, down from 17 degrees C four weeks ago
- Measured aeration basin alkalinity: 84 mg/L as CaCO3
- Nitrate-N reduced in the anoxic zone: not measured
- Supplied factors for this example: 7.14 mg CaCO3 per mg NH3-N oxidized; 3.57 mg CaCO3 per mg NO3-N reduced

Record to reject: a shift log entry states "sludge age 14 days, nitrification capacity adequate, no action." The spreadsheet behind that entry divides total plant solids inventory, including clarifier and aerobic digester, by WAS mass only, and it omits effluent solids. It is unsupported for a nitrification question. A second log entry claims "anoxic zone returning 30 mg/L alkalinity" with no nitrate data behind it, so that credit is also rejected.

Worked solution:

Aerobic inventory: 2,000 m3 x 2,150 g/m3 = 4,300,000 g = 4,300 kg
WAS solids: 78 m3/d x 6.4 kg/m3 = 499.2 kg/d
Effluent solids: 5,400 m3/d x 0.015 kg/m3 = 81.0 kg/d
Total out: 499.2 kg/d + 81.0 kg/d = 580.2 kg/d
Aerobic SRT: 4,300 kg / 580.2 kg/d = 7.41 d, not 14 d

Nitrogen load: 26 g N/m3 x 5,400 m3/d = 140,400 g N/d = 140.4 kg N/d
Theoretical alkalinity demand: 26 mg/L x 7.14 = 185.6 mg/L as CaCO3
Theoretical residual: 190 mg/L - 185.6 mg/L = 4.4 mg/L as CaCO3, with no verified denitrification credit

Ranking: measured basin alkalinity of 84 mg/L as CaCO3 is well above the 4.4 mg/L screening residual, which means unmeasured recovery or return alkalinity exists, so the calculation is a flag rather than proof. Two explanations lead: aerobic SRT of 7.41 d against an 11.5 degrees C mixed liquor, and possible alkalinity or pH stress. Distinguishing tests: measure anoxic zone nitrate-N and basin pH on the same shift, and trend alkalinity daily for one week before any wasting change is made under the approved procedure.

checks.prompt: In this module, what does the supplied teaching factor of 3.57 mg CaCO3 per mg nitrate-N reduced represent?

About 3.57 times
checks.explanation: Nitrate reported as NO3 is roughly 4.43 times the same sample reported as NO3-N. The 1.22 factor belongs to ammonia reported as NH3 versus NH3-N, so using it here would understate the nitrate basis difference badly.

checks.prompt: Operators at a fictional plant suspect an increased nitrogen load is behind higher effluent ammonia-N. Which check best distinguishes that explanation from the others?
choices: Compare influent ammonia-N concentration on two grab samples
Recalculate influent nitrogen as kg N/d over 7 to 10 days
Raise the aeration blower setpoint and watch ammonia respond
Compare clarifier sludge blanket depth against last month
checks.explanation: Load is a mass question, so flow-weighted kg N/d over a week or more separates a real load increase from dilution or concentration noise. Two grab concentrations can move purely with flow and prove nothing about mass arriving.

modules.title: Monitored recovery and reassessment
